title: Miri and piri as thought
hook: spiritual and worldly life held together, not split

segments.voice: Yesterday, Granth and Panth: the Guru carried by a book and by a people. Your line was book and people. Whom did you share a good line with? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-seven.

Two swords, worn at once. That is how Sikh tradition remembers Guru Hargobind on the day he took up the guruship: not one sword but two, one at each side. When people asked why, the answer came in a pair of words. One sword for miri. One sword for piri. It is easy to live as if life comes in two drawers. One drawer for the job, the rent, the news, the arguments about who does the dishes. Another drawer, smaller, for prayer or quiet or whatever we call the sacred. Today's lesson is about refusing the two drawers. Not the swords themselves, but the thought behind them.
screen: `TWO SWORDS, WORN AT ONCE.` → `MIRI. PIRI.` → `NOT TWO DRAWERS.`

segments.voice: First, the words. Miri is worldly authority: the life of rule, justice, work, the public square. Piri is spiritual authority: the life of prayer, the Word, the inner path. Second, the picture tradition keeps. Alongside the two swords, tradition says Guru Hargobind raised the Akal Takht, a seat of worldly authority, facing the Harmandir, the house of prayer. Two buildings, looking at each other. Not one behind the other. Not one in a different city. Facing. Third, the Granth underneath the picture. The idea didn't start with the swords. Guru Arjan, in the var in Raag Gujri, says it with ordinary words. In paraphrase: meeting the true Guru, a person finds the complete way, and is set free while laughing, playing, dressing and eating. Notice the verbs. Laughing. Playing. Getting dressed. Eating. Liberation isn't kept in a separate room for special occasions. It happens in the middle of the ordinary. Fourth, what the thought asks of a person. If miri and piri belong together, then prayer has to show up at work, and work has to be done as if the Guru were watching. Sikh teachers read the two swords as a call to care about justice as a spiritual duty, and to keep the inner life awake while doing it. A prayer that never touches how you treat people stays in the drawer. A public life with no inner life loses its way. The thought refuses both. Both together.
screen: `MIRI: THE WORLD. PIRI: THE SPIRIT.` · `TWO BUILDINGS, FACING.` · `FREE WHILE LAUGHING AND EATING.` · `PRAYER AT WORK; WORK AS PRAYER.` · then, large: `BOTH TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring prayer to a practical task. Settle, and breathe. Pick the next ordinary task you'll do after this: dishes, an email, a drive, a diaper, a spreadsheet. See yourself doing it. Now, without changing the task at all, bring this sit with you into it. The same breath. The same quiet. If you pray, you can hold Waheguru in the back of your mind while your hands do the work. If you don't, carry one steady breath into it. Same task. Different drawer. Actually, no drawer at all. The bell holds the time.
Miri and piri as thought. Worldly life and spiritual life held together, not split: two swords, two buildings facing, one life. Today's word.
screen: `MIRI AND PIRI AS THOUGHT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: both together. Today, do one piece of ordinary work with the same care you'd bring to prayer. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of miri and piri, worldly and spiritual authority, as held together, remembered in Guru Hargobind's two swords and in the Akal Takht facing the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar.

fork.setup: you're the new Guru, and you want to show that the spiritual and the worldly belong together. tradition says you do what?
options: wear one sword and leave prayer to others.
give up all worldly power and retreat to pray.
wear two swords, one for miri and one for piri.
fork.reveal: Sikh tradition remembers Guru Hargobind wearing two swords, and raising the Akal Takht facing the Harmandir.
